mcqs.question: A raw, unformatted disk block device already durably stores bytes across reboots. What does a file system add on top of that?
options: Naming and organization — turning numbered blocks into paths, directories, and metadata
Durability — without a file system, data would not survive a power cycle at all
The ability to store more total bytes than the raw device physically has
Encryption of all data by default
mcqs.explanation: Raw blocks are already persistent; what's missing is naming, organization, and bookkeeping (inodes, directories, free-space maps). A file system doesn't increase raw capacity or encrypt by default.

mcqs.question: You run `chmod 644 report.txt` without touching its content. Which timestamp changes?
options: mtime only, since chmod is a modification
atime only, since the file was accessed to check permissions
ctime only, since metadata changed but content did not
Both mtime and ctime, since any change touches both
mcqs.explanation: ctime tracks metadata changes (permissions, ownership, link count); mtime tracks content changes. A permission-only change bumps ctime but leaves mtime untouched — a classic interview trap.

mcqs.question: Why is `mv file.txt /same/disk/newname.txt` nearly instant regardless of file size, while `cp` of the same file takes time proportional to its size?
options: mv compresses the file before moving it
mv is instant because it only works on empty files
mv only updates the directory entry pointing to the inode; the data blocks never move
The kernel caches all files smaller than 1GB in RAM automatically
mcqs.explanation: A rename on the same file system just repoints a directory entry to the same inode — no data blocks are touched. Copying must read and write every block, so its cost scales with file size.

mcqs.question: A program processes a 4GB log file strictly from start to end, never jumping around. On an HDD-backed system, why does this pattern perform well?
options: Sequential access always fits entirely in RAM
The OS automatically converts sequential reads into random reads for speed
HDDs only support sequential access, so this is the only pattern that works at all
The disk arm doesn't need to seek repeatedly — it tracks forward with the data as it streams
mcqs.explanation: Sequential access avoids repeated seeks, which dominate HDD latency (milliseconds each). It has nothing to do with fitting in RAM, and HDDs fully support random access — just slowly.

mcqs.question: A process holds `app.log` open and keeps writing to it. Another process runs `rm app.log`, and `df` shows no space freed. Why?
options: rm silently failed and the file still has its original name
The directory entry was removed, but the inode and blocks stay allocated while a process still has it open
Space is only freed after a full disk defragmentation
rm only works on files smaller than the free space bitmap page size
mcqs.explanation: unlink() removes the name, but the inode persists as long as its link count or open-descriptor count is nonzero. The writing process still holds a descriptor, so the space stays allocated until it closes the file.
